claim: Continuous rewiring of synaptic connections may exchange up to 50% of the synapse population over a time-course of weeks.
source: Continuous rewiring of the synaptic connections (Holtmaat et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009; Loewenstein et al., 2015) may exchange up to 50% of the synapse population over a time-course of weeks (Loewenstein et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies, particularly Loewenstein et al., 2015.

claim: Only a minuscule fraction of synaptic connections generated upon original learning persists after a few months.
source: Hence, only a minuscule fraction of synaptic connections generated upon the original learning experience persists after a few months (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claim: Despite continuous synaptic turnover, memories are not only stable but might even improve without further training.
source: Intriguingly, experiments demonstrate that despite this continuous synaptic turnover, memories are not only stable but might even improve without further training (Walker et al., 2003; Cai and Rickard, 2009; Honma et al., 2015), especially during sleep (Jenkins and Dallenbach, 1924; Karni et al., 1994; Fischer et al., 2002; Walker et al., 2003; Dudai, 2004; Stickgold, 2005; Gais et al., 2006; Korman et al., 2007; Lahl et al., 2008; Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Pan and Rickard, 2015; Rickard and Pan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: One hypothesis for memory retention is that there are two pools of synapses: a stable and an unstable one.
source: One hypothesis is that there are two pools of synapses: a stable and an unstable one (Kasai et al., 2003; Loewenstein et al., 2015), and in particular inhibitory stability could play a crucial role (Mongillo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kasai et al., 2003, Loewenstein et al., 2015, and Mongillo et al., 2018.

claim: Periodic external replay of learned input patterns strengthens synaptic connections that are consistent with existing connections.
source: For example, Acker et al. (2018) show that periodic, external replay of learned input patterns strengthens synaptic connections that are consistent with existing connections.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Acker et al., 2018.

claim: Hippocampal replay does not appear to be necessary to maintain cortical memories, as shown by the case of patient H.M.
source: However, as the case of patient H.M. shows, hippocampal replay does not appear to be necessary to maintain cortical memories.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the well-known case of patient H.M.

claim: Spontaneous alternation between high and low population activity has been associated with Up-Down-dynamics observed in cortical networks during sleep.
source: Such spontaneous alternation between high and low population activity has previously been associated with Up-Down-dynamics (Holcman and Tsodyks, 2006; Barak and Tsodyks, 2007; Setareh et al., 2017; Jercog et al., 2017), observed in cortical networks during sleep (Steriade et al., 1993) and in quiescent awake states (Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Okun et al., 2010; Engel et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental and modeling studies.

claim: Learning- and memory-related activity patterns are reactivated in cortex, predominantly during sleep and rest.
source: Along these lines, experiments show that learning- and memory-related activity patterns are reactivated in cortex, predominantly during sleep and rest (Peyrache et al., 2009; Gulati et al., 2014; Ramanathan et al., 2015; Gulati et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: Larger synapses are less likely to be removed than smaller synapses.
source: In particular, larger synapses are less likely to be removed (e.g. Le Bé and Markram, 2006) implying that rewiring follows synaptic plasticity and attains Hebbian-like character.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Le Bé and Markram, 2006.

claim: The combination of structural plasticity, synaptic plasticity and self-generated reactivation can stabilize assemblies against synaptic turnover and enhance their connectivity and associative memory.
source: Here, we show that the combination of structural plasticity, synaptic plasticity and self-generated reactivation, even for a just short period every day, can not only stabilize assemblies against synaptic turnover but even enhance their connectivity and associative memory.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the computational modeling results presented throughout.

claim: During the learning phase, each stimulated group becomes a highly interconnected cell assembly.
source: In summary, during the learning phase, each stimulated group becomes a highly interconnected cell assembly, while all non-intra-assembly synapses remain sparse and have small synaptic weights (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The synaptic connectivity follows the synaptic strength on a time-scale of hours.
source: The synaptic connectivity follows the synaptic strength on a time-scale of hours.
evidence: The claim is based on the simulation results showing the temporal dynamics of weights and connectivity.

claim: During sensory phases, lateral inhibition prevents spontaneous activation of non-stimulated neurons and the assemblies slowly decay.
source: During sensory phases, the network receives stimulation with quickly changing random patterns mimicking incoming information from upstream networks. In this phase, lateral inhibition prevents spontaneous activation of non-stimulated neurons and the assemblies slowly decay.
evidence: The claim is based on the model design and simulation results.

claim: During rest phases, assemblies can reactivate provided there is sufficient intra-assembly recurrence.
source: However, during rest phases, stimulation is absent and the assemblies can reactivate. This happens provided there is sufficient intra-assembly recurrence, so that the positive feedback drives the assemblies towards a high population activity (e.g. Wilson and Cowan, 1972; Brunel, 2000; Figure 3A, black nullcline), which corresponds to a reactivation of the learned pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data and theoretical considerations, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Lateral inhibition implements a winner-take-all structure such that only one assembly reactivates at any time.
source: As lateral inhibition implements a winner-take-all structure, only one of the assemblies reactivates at any time.
evidence: The claim is based on the model design and known properties of lateral inhibition.

claim: For connections within the same assembly, the activity is strongly correlated during rest phases.
source: For connections within the same assembly, the activity is strongly correlated (Figure 3Ci).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3Ci.

claim: For connections between pairs of neurons from different assemblies or from assembly and control group there is virtually no correlated activity during rest phases.
source: In contrast, for connections between pairs of neurons from different assemblies or from assembly and control group there is virtually no correlated activity (Figure 3Cii).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3Cii.

claim: Short-term depression weakens the transmission efficacy of excitatory synapses and thereby the positive feedback, causing the high population activity to become unstable.
source: Similar to other models (Barak and Tsodyks, 2007; Holcman and Tsodyks, 2006), short-term depression weakens the transmission efficacy of the excitatory synapses and thereby the positive feedback. As a consequence, the high population activity becomes unstable (i.e. the high activity fixed-point vanishes, Figure 3A, grey nullcline) such that the activity drops back and the synapses can recover.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model mechanism and citations to similar models, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Without rest phases in which assemblies can reactivate, synaptic weights inside assemblies decay.
source: If there are no rest phases in which the assemblies can reactivate, the synaptic weights inside the assemblies decay (Figure 4A, Top).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Synaptic weight decay is followed by a decay in the number of synapses on a timescale of days.
source: Because the synaptic removal rate is faster for small synapses, the synaptic weight decay is followed by a decay in the number of synapses on a timescale of days (Figure 4A, Bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4A and the model's structural plasticity rule.

claim: When sensory phases are interleaved with rest phases, the strong connectivity inside the assembly is not only preserved but even gradually increases.
source: In contrast, when the sensory phases are interleaved with rest phases, we observe that the strong connectivity inside the assembly is not only preserved by the self-reactivations, but even gradually increases (Figure 4B, Bottom, purple curve).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Connectivity from and to other assemblies in the network remains weak when sensory phases are interleaved with rest phases.
source: Moreover, the connectivity from and to other assemblies in the network remains weak (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Spurious connections built up during sensory phases are removed during rest phases.
source: Close inspection of the connectivity changes reveals that also spurious connections that were built-up during the sensory phases are removed during the rest phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of structural plasticity during retention, assemblies initially reactivate and are stable for multiple days, but a long sensory phase can drive them below the reactivation threshold causing all assemblies to be lost.
source: In the absence of structural plasticity, maintaining the memories is more challenging. In Figure 4D, we blocked structural plasticity during the retention phase. The assemblies initially reactivate and are stable for multiple days, but a long sensory phase after 100 hours drives them below the reactivation threshold and all assemblies are lost.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The model exhibits ongoing synapse creation and removal within assemblies, exchanging around 10% of the synapse population on a daily basis.
source: Similar to experiments (Holtmaat et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2009; Loewenstein et al., 2015), we measured the persistence of synapses at a specific potential synaptic locations from day to day and find ongoing synapse creation and removal within the assemblies, exchanging around 10% of the synapse population on a daily basis (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5A and comparison to experimental studies.

claim: Synapse creation transiently increases shortly after learning while spine removal remains low, similar to experiments.
source: Moreover, synapse creation transiently increases shortly after learning while spine removal remains low, similar as in experiments (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data and citation to Yang et al., 2014.

claim: The fraction of synapses present after learning that persist until a given time-point continuously decreases.
source: The fraction of synapses that were present after learning and persist until a given time-point continuously decreases (Figure 5B) indicating that also strong synapses inside the assemblies are continuously removed.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The strengthening of assemblies emerges because reactivations stabilize more synapses than are being removed, resulting in continuous exchange of the synaptic substrate.
source: Hence, the strengthening of the assemblies is not emerging from a simple addition of new synapses, but because the reactivations stabilize more synapses than are being removed and thus the synaptic substrate of the assemblies is continuously exchanged (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation data, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Self-induced strengthening improves recall quality.
source: In summary, the self-induced strengthening improves recall quality.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the pattern completion analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: The number of connections in an assembly increases more the longer the rest phases and the shorter the sensory phases.
source: Starting from a given number of synapses between the neurons in the assembly, we find that the number of connections increases more the longer the rest phases and the shorter sensory phases (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A simple theory assuming all synapses in an assembly are maximally potentiated by reactivation during rest and decay exponentially during sensory phases explains the simulation results over a broad regime of timescales.
source: This simple theory explains the simulation results over a broad regime of timescales (Figure 7B) indicating that the dynamics of the intra-assembly synapses is governed by the collective reactivation of the assemblies.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of theoretical predictions with simulation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The larger the number of initial connections, the longer assemblies survive without reactivation.
source: Unsurprisingly, the larger the number of initial connections, the longer the assemblies survive (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: By increasing their connectivity through self-reactivation, assemblies become more stable against prolonged absence of reactivation.
source: This, in turn, implies that by increasing their connectivity by self-reactivation, the assemblies also become more and more stable against prolonged absence of reactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the simulation results showing the relationship between connectivity and survival time.

claim: Connections in an assembly can either decay to control levels or converge to a fixed number of synapses.
source: Connections in an anssembly can undergo two fates: either the connections decay to control levels or they converge to a fixed number of synapses (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The number of synapses either decreases for large initial numbers and increases for small initial numbers, converging to a stationary final value after many cycles.
source: The number of synapses either decreases for large initial numbers of synapses and increases for small initial numbers of synapses, matching theory (Figure 7F). Hence, after many cycles with the same phase durations, the number of synapses will converge and fluctuate around a stationary final value (gray line).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data and theoretical predictions shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: The longer the rest phase and the shorter the sensory phase, the higher the stationary value of synapses.
source: The theory provides the dependence of this final value on the durations of sensory and rest phases: The longer the rest phase and the shorter the sensory the higher the value (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical predictions shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Even a short rest phase of 3 min is sufficient to maintain strong connectivity for up to 20 hr of sensory phase.
source: Note, however, even a short rest phase of 3 min is sufficient to maintain strong connectivity for up to 20 hr of sensory phase.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the theoretical predictions shown in Figure 7G.

claim: A network with short-term depression maintained overlapping assemblies after 5 days.
source: After 5 days, the network with short-term depression maintained the overlapping assemblies (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A network with spike-frequency adaptation formed non-overlapping assemblies, with neurons in the overlapping population incorporated into either one of the assemblies.
source: In contrast, the network with spike-frequency adaptation has formed non-overlapping assemblies (Figure 8B) and the neurons in the overlapping population have been incorporated into either one of the assemblies.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: With spike-frequency adaptation, neurons activated with the first assembly will be adapted and less likely to be reactivated with the second assembly, leading to separation of overlapping assemblies.
source: The reason for the difference is that with spike-frequency adaptation, neurons activated with the first assembly will be adapted and therefore less likely to be reactivated with second assembly. Due to this competition and the positive feedback between activity and connectivity introduced by the Hebbian plasticity processes, the overlap region will be reactivated and connected more and more with only one of the assemblies and disconnect from the other, separating the assemblies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model mechanisms and simulation results.

claim: Using short-term depression, only the synapses between the overlap region and the assembly are adapted such that reactivation with another assembly is not impeded.
source: In contrast, using short-term depression, only the synapses between the overlap region and the assembly are adapted such that a reactivation with another assembly is not impeded.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model mechanisms.

claim: During random sensory stimulation, cell assemblies decay.
source: During random sensory stimulation these assemblies decay, but in the absence of external stimulation, the cell assemblies self-reactivate resulting in periods of strong correlated activity which strengthen and stabilize the intra-assembly connectivity, and weaken other connections.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by simulation data throughout the paper.

claim: In the absence of external stimulation, cell assemblies self-reactivate resulting in periods of strong correlated activity which strengthen and stabilize intra-assembly connectivity and weaken other connections.
source: During random sensory stimulation these assemblies decay, but in the absence of external stimulation, the cell assemblies self-reactivate resulting in periods of strong correlated activity which strengthen and stabilize the intra-assembly connectivity, and weaken other connections.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by simulation data throughout the paper.

claim: Self-reactivation protects assemblies against ongoing synaptic turnover.
source: This protects the assemblies against ongoing synaptic turnover, increases their robustness against prolonged phases without reactivation, and leads to off-line improvement of the associative properties of the memories.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results presented throughout the paper.

claim: Self-reactivation increases assembly robustness against prolonged phases without reactivation.
source: This protects the assemblies against ongoing synaptic turnover, increases their robustness against prolonged phases without reactivation, and leads to off-line improvement of the associative properties of the memories.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results, particularly those shown in Figure 7.

claim: Self-reactivation leads to offline improvement of the associative properties of memories.
source: This protects the assemblies against ongoing synaptic turnover, increases their robustness against prolonged phases without reactivation, and leads to off-line improvement of the associative properties of the memories.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results, particularly those shown in Figure 6.

claim: The network needs to be able to spontaneously reactivate assemblies, requiring sufficient increase of synaptic weights during learning for net positive feedback.
source: The critical ingredients and parameters for the mechanism to work are as follows: (1) The network needs to be able to spontaneously reactivate assemblies. This requires sufficient increase of the synaptic weights during the learning phase, so that the assembly has a net positive feedback and can transition to a high activity state.
evidence: The claim describes a critical requirement of the model mechanism.

claim: The high activity state needs to terminate, requiring an adaptive mechanism such as spike frequency adaptation or short-term synaptic depression.
source: (2) The high activity state needs to terminate, requiring an adaptive mechanism such as spike frequency adaptation or short-term synaptic depression.
evidence: The claim describes a critical requirement of the model mechanism.

claim: Lateral inhibition is required to prevent activation from spreading to multiple assemblies and to decorrelate activity.
source: (3) Lateral inhibition is required to prevent the activation from spreading to multiple assemblies. This de-correlates activity and ensures that only connections within the assemblies potentiate.
evidence: The claim describes a critical requirement of the model mechanism.

claim: Structural plasticity should encourage stabilization of intra-assembly synapses.
source: (4) Structural plasticity should encourage stabilization of intra-assembly synapses. Here, this is achieved by a higher synapses removal rate for small synapses, while the synapse creation rate is fixed.
evidence: The claim describes a critical requirement of the model mechanism.

claim: The structural plasticity in the model is not associative by itself but becomes so indirectly via its dependence on synaptic weights.
source: Note, that the the structural plasticity in our model is not associative by itself. It becomes so indirectly via its dependence on the synaptic weights.
evidence: The claim clarifies a property of the model mechanism.

claim: Connections between assemblies should remain weak, which requires synaptic plasticity that depresses weights in case of asynchronous high pre- and postsynaptic activity.
source: (5) Connections between assemblies should remain weak, which, given (3) and (4), requires synaptic plasticity which depresses weights in case of asynchronous high pre- and postsynaptic activity, as is the case in Hebbian learning.
evidence: The claim describes a critical requirement of the model mechanism.

claim: Previous models have used reactivation to strengthen or restructure previously stored memories but often rely on external reactivation mechanisms.
source: A number of earlier models of long-term and very-long-term memory have used reactivation to strengthen or restructure previously stored memories. However, these models often rely on an external reactivation mechanism (Tetzlaff et al., 2013; Acker et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: In the current model, self-generated reactivations cause non-correlated reactivations of individual cell assemblies, such that neither individual external cues nor pre-structured connectivity are necessary.
source: In contrast, here the self-generated reactivations of cell assemblies cause non-correlated reactivations of individual cell assemblies, such that neither individual external cues (Acker et al., 2018), nor pre-structured connectivity (Tetzlaff et al., 2011; Tetzlaff et al., 2013) are necessary.
evidence: The claim contrasts the current model with previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Other models have shown that self-organized reactivation can stabilize Hebbian cell assemblies against ongoing synaptic plasticity, but stability was only demonstrated on a timescale of hours and in the absence of synaptic turnover.
source: Other models have shown that self-organized reactivation can stabilize Hebbian cell assemblies against ongoing synaptic plasticity (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Zenke et al., 2015). However, stability was only demonstrated on a timescale of hours and in the absence of synaptic turnover.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: In the current model, assemblies can survive for many hours without reactivation.
source: Here, we show that assemblies can indeed survive for many hours without reactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the current model, reactivations maintain and strengthen assembly connectivity by stabilizing new synapses which support memories while removing distracting synapses, resulting in offline memory gains.
source: Moreover, in our model, reactivations maintain and strengthen the assembly connectivity by stabilizing new synapses which support the memories, while removing distracting synapses, resulting in offline memory gains.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by simulation data throughout the paper.

claim: Offline memory gains will generally emerge for mechanisms which induce a bi-stable connectivity dynamics.
source: We expect that offline memory gains will generally emerge for mechanisms which induce a bi-stable connectivity dynamics, that is when synapse creation balances removal both in a weakly and a strongly connected configuration and connectivity will converge to one of these configurations from any initial condition (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: The claim is a generalization based on the model results and theoretical analysis.

claim: Bi-stability in connectivity dynamics does not necessarily have to rely on reactivation.
source: For example, the bi-stablility does not necessarily have to rely on reactivation (see Helias, 2008; Deger et al., 2012; Fauth et al., 2015; Deger et al., 2018 for alternatives).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to alternative mechanisms.

claim: As connectivity dynamics in the presence of structural plasticity is slow, memory strength will typically not be saturated after learning.
source: However, as connectivity dynamics in the presence of structural plasticity is slow, memory strength will typically not be saturated after learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model properties.

claim: Whenever the memory is strong enough, one should observe convergence to the upper configuration and hence a strengthening after learning.
source: Therefore whenever the memory is strong enough, one should observe convergence to the upper configuration and hence a strengthening after learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the bi-stable dynamics analysis.

claim: When only faster synaptic plasticity is considered for memory formation, connectivity tends to converge already during learning and no offline strengthening will be observed.
source: However, when only faster synaptic plasticity is considered for memory formation, the connectivity (i.e. the weights) tends to converge already during learning and no off-line strengthening will be observed (Zenke et al., 2015; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; but see Figure 6 in Tetzlaff et al., 2013 for an example of non-converged weights).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: Reactivations of memory related activity patterns in cortex have been reported mostly during sleep, predominantly during NREM or slow-wave sleep.
source: Reactivations of memory related activity patterns in cortex have been reported mostly during sleep, predominantly during NREM or slow-wave sleep (Ramanathan et al., 2015; Gulati et al., 2017; Gulati et al., 2014; Peyrache et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: During slow-wave sleep, the cortex exhibits alternating phases of high and low activity, called Up- and Down-phases or slow oscillations.
source: During this sleep phase, the cortex exhibits alternating phases of high and low activity, so-called Up- and Down-phases or slow oscillations (Steriade et al., 1993; Steriade et al., 2001; Timofeev et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Up-Down-dynamics relies on recurrent excitation.
source: This Up-Down-dynamics relies on recurrent excitation (Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000), similar to the dynamics here.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work and comparison to the model.

claim: In vitro imaging of individual activity during Up-Down-dynamics in cortical slices reveals that each Up-state comprises a subgroup of cells with strong correlated activity.
source: In vitro imaging of individual activity during Up-Down-dynamics in cortical slices reveal further similarities with our model: Each Up-state comprises a subgroup of cells with strong correlated activity and the time-course of the activity is reminiscent of the convergence into an attractive state (Cossart et al., 2003; Shu et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In vivo, Up-states induce stereotypical local patterns.
source: Accordingly, also in vivo, Up-states induce stereotypical local patterns (Luczak et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Single-cell recordings indicate that learning-related activity patterns reactivate during slow-wave sleep and that this is phase-coupled with Up-states.
source: Finally, single-cell recordings indicate that learning-related activity patterns reactivate during slow-wave sleep and that this is phase-coupled with Up-states (Ramanathan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The memory strengthening reported in the model might be related to the long known beneficial properties of sleep on memory.
source: The memory strengthening reported here might therefore be related to the long known beneficial properties of sleep on memory (Jenkins and Dallenbach, 1924; Karni et al., 1994; Fischer et al., 2002; Walker et al., 2003; Dudai, 2004; Stickgold, 2005; Gais et al., 2006; Korman et al., 2007; Lahl et al., 2008; Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Pan and Rickard, 2015; Rickard and Pan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting model results to experimental observations via citations.

claim: In the model, there is a decrease of memory stability for very long wake (sensory) phases.
source: In our model, we observe a decrease of memory stability for very long wake (sensory) phases (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 7.

claim: As sleep deprivation normally does not lead to large scale loss of memories, there may be further processes at work to prevent memory decay.
source: However, as sleep deprivation normally does not lead to a large scale loss of memories, it is possible that there are further processes at work to prevent the decay of memories.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on general knowledge about sleep deprivation effects.

claim: There may be a stable pool of synapses which is more resilient to decay.
source: For example, there may be a stable pool of synapses (Kasai et al., 2003; Loewenstein et al., 2015), which is more resilient to decay.
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Reactivations do not exclusively occur during sleep, as sleep-like activity patterns can also be observed during periods of resting or quiet wakefulness.
source: Another possibility is that reactivations do not exclusively occur during sleep, as sleep-like activity patterns can also be observed during periods of resting or quiet wakefulness (Vyazovskiy et al., 2011; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Engel et al., 2016; Gentet et al., 2010; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Okun et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Offline-gains for some kinds of memories have been observed during wakefulness.
source: Coherent with the above-presented model, offline-gains for some kinds of memories have been observed during wakefulness (Walker et al., 2003; Rickard et al., 2008; Cai and Rickard, 2009; Varga et al., 2014; Honma et al., 2015; Pan and Rickard, 2015; Rickard and Pan, 2017 but see, for example Adi-Japha and Karni, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Several fMRI studies establish a link between the reactivation of task specific patterns during rest periods and later task performance.
source: Moreover, several fMRI studies establish a link between the reactivation of task specific patterns during rest periods and later task performance (Staresina et al., 2013; Deuker et al., 2013), which is consistent with this view.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The synaptic homeostasis hypothesis states that connectivity should be down-regulated during sleep to balance the potentiation dominated wake intervals and to allow for new learning.
source: On one hand, the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis states that connectivity should be down-regulated during sleep to balance the potentiation dominated wake intervals and to allow for new learning (Tononi and Cirelli, 2003; Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis.

claim: There is accumulating evidence that connectivity is built-up especially after learning.
source: On the other hand, there is accumulating evidence that connectivity is built-up especially after learning (e.g. Yang et al., 2014, for a recent review see Timofeev and Chauvette, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies and reviews.

claim: In the model, there is an increase in intra-assembly connectivity during rest phases.
source: Here, we observe an increase in the intra-assembly connectivity, consistent with the second hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown throughout the paper.

claim: In the model, inter-assembly and control connectivity decreases during rest phases.
source: Yet, inter-assembly and control connectivity decreases, as proposed by the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model combines and refines both views: connectivity inside memory representations is up-regulated while the rest of the network down-regulates weights and number of synapses.
source: Thus, our model combines and refines both views: connectivity inside memory representations is up-regulated, such that memories are consolidated and strengthened, whereas the rest of of the network down-regulates weights and number of synapses, such that these neurons remain susceptible to subsequent learning.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Large intrinsic fluctuations of synaptic weights are observed on a daily basis in experiments.
source: Most prominent are the large intrinsic fluctuations of the synaptic weights observed on a daily basis (Yasumatsu et al., 2008; Statman et al., 2014; Dvorkin and Ziv, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The daily changes of synaptic weights in the model are comparable to experimental data.
source: Although the daily changes of the synaptic weights in our model are comparable to experimental data, in the model the synapses segregrate in a stable and unstable pool (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, compare to Yasumatsu et al., 2008, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation data to experimental data.

claim: In the model, synapses segregate into a stable and unstable pool.
source: Although the daily changes of the synaptic weights in our model are comparable to experimental data, in the model the synapses segregrate in a stable and unstable pool (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, compare to Yasumatsu et al., 2008, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: It needs to be clarified in future research how synapse intrinsic fluctuations affect memory maintenance.
source: It needs to be clarified in future research how such synapse intrinsic fluctuations affect memory maintenance.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Connectivity build-up due to self-reactivation is expected to make memories more robust even in the context of synapse intrinsic fluctuations.
source: We expect that also in this context the connectivity build-up due self-reactivation will make memories more robust.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about expected behavior.
